summary: Defines signature policies for electronic signatures. A policy is a set of rules for creating and validating a signature, and a legal or contractual context may accept one as meeting its needs. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: It is a rulebook saying what counts as a good signature, so everyone agrees whether a signed paper is valid.

questions: what is an electronic signature policy
what is a signature policy identifier
how does a verifier use a signature policy
what is a signature validation policy
subtitle: A written and machine-readable rulebook that says exactly when an electronic signature counts as valid.

tldr.problem: Two parties checking the same electronic signature can reach different answers unless they agree on the rules, and a legal or contractual setting needs to know which rules a signature was made under.
tldr.mechanism: A signature policy is a set of rules with a globally unique object identifier. The signer binds that identifier to the signature, and the verifier validates under the same rules. The RFC defines an optional ASN.1 structure so the rules can be processed by computer.
tldr.outcome: Signer and verifier follow one definitive policy, whose hash is provided by the signer and checked by the verifier. This is an Experimental specification, based on ETSI TS 101 733 V.1.2.2.

today: RFC 3125 is an Experimental specification and, in the data given here, is neither obsoleted nor updated. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: What a Signature Policy Is
sections.content:
A signature policy is a set of rules for creating and validating an electronic signature, under which the validity of the signature can be determined. A given legal or contractual context may recognize a particular policy as meeting its requirements.

Each policy has a globally unique reference, and the signer binds that reference to the signature as part of the signature calculation. The policy needs a human readable form so that it can be assessed against the legal and contractual context, and a computer processable form so signatures can be handled automatically. This document defines that second form using ASN.1.

The document is independent of any environment. The RFC names smart cards, GSM SIM cards and special programs as examples of where it can be applied. Its content is based on the signature policy defined in ETSI TS 101 733 V.1.2.2.
sections.eli5: Imagine a game where everyone must agree on the rules before playing. A signature policy is that rulebook for signing papers, with a name tag on it so everyone knows which rulebook was used.

sections.title: The Parties Involved
sections.content:
The RFC names five kinds of party:

  • The Signature Policy Issuer issues policies that define the technical and procedural requirements for creating and validating signatures for a particular business need.
  • The Signer creates the signature. By signing over the policy identifier, the signer commits that the data was signed under that policy's rules.
  • The Verifier validates the signature, and MUST do so under the rules of the policy for the signature to be valid.
  • The Arbitrator settles disputes between signer and verifier, and acts as a verifier when it checks a signature that was already validated.
  • Trusted Service Providers help build trust between signer and verifier. These include certification authorities, registration authorities, repository authorities, time-stamping authorities, OCSP responders and attribute authorities.

A policy may require the use of particular trusted services, such as user certificates, cross-certificates, time-stamp tokens, CRLs, ARLs and OCSP responses.
sections.eli5: There is a person who writes the rulebook, one who signs, one who checks, a judge for arguments, and helpers like a clock-keeper and an ID office that both sides can trust.

sections.title: How a Policy Is Specified
sections.content:
The RFC mandates five things. A signature must be processed by signer and verifier under the policy the signer referenced. That policy must be identifiable by an Object Identifier. A specification of it must exist. There must be one definitive form of that specification with a unique binary encoding. And a hash of the definitive specification, using an agreed algorithm, must be provided by the signer and checked by the verifier.

The form of the specification is defined but not mandated. A policy can be a free-form document for people or a structured form using an agreed syntax. The ASN.1 structure in this RFC is optional and is encoded with the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER).

Its top level SignaturePolicy holds a hash algorithm identifier, the SignPolicyInfo and an optional hash value. The hash is recalculated and checked whenever the policy passes between issuer and signer or verifier. Inside SignPolicyInfo are the policy identifier, the date of issue, the issuer name, the field of application and the signature validation policy.
sections.eli5: The rulebook has a title page with its unique name, who wrote it and when, plus a special fingerprint of the whole book. If someone changes a page, the fingerprint no longer matches and everybody can tell.

sections.title: Validation Rules in the Structure
sections.content:
The signature validation policy says which data elements a signature must contain to be potentially valid. It has a signingPeriod, giving a notBefore time before which the policy SHOULD NOT be used and an optional notAfter, plus commonRules and commitmentRules.

Common rules apply to every commitment type, and commitment rules apply to particular commitment types. If a field is in the common rules, it must not appear in any commitment rule. Signer and verifier rules, the signing certificate trust condition and the time-stamp trust condition must be present either in the common rules or in every commitment rule. A given commitment type identifier must not appear in more than one commitment rule.

Signer rules say which CMS signed and unsigned attributes the signer must provide, and whether the signer must reference and include only its own certificate or the full path to a trust point. Verifier rules list unsigned attributes the verifier must add if the signer did not.
sections.eli5: Some rules apply to every kind of signing, like a school rule. Others apply only to certain kinds, like a rule just for the science lab, and the same rule is never written in both places.

sections.title: Certificates, Revocation, Time-Stamps and Algorithms
sections.content:
Trust conditions are built from CertificateTrustTrees, a list of self-signed trust points where certificate path checking starts. Each trust point can limit the path with pathLenConstraint (zero means only the trust point and an end-entity certificate), list acceptable certificate policies, and restrict names or policy mapping.

Revocation requirements say how status must be checked, with values for checking CRLs, OCSP, both, either, no check, or another mechanism defined by an extension. These can be set separately for end certificates and CA certificates. The same machinery applies to the signing certificate, the time-stamping authority and attribute certificates.

The time-stamp trust condition can set a cautionPeriod, a wait after signing before revocation information may be used to validate, and a signatureTimestampDelay, the maximum acceptable time between signing and the signature time-stamp. The attribute trust condition can require claimed attributes, certified attributes or either. Algorithm constraints name the hash, public key or combined algorithms allowed for the signer, issuers and authorities, with an optional minimum key length in bits.

New rules can be added through SignPolExtensions, each with its own object identifier and a defined syntax and meaning.
sections.eli5: The rulebook can say which ID offices you trust, how to check an ID has not been cancelled, how soon a signature must be stamped with the time, and which kinds of locks are strong enough.

sections.title: Security and Conformance
sections.content:
The RFC makes two security points. The security of the whole mechanism depends on the privacy of the signer's private key, and implementations must take steps so that private keys cannot be compromised. Cryptographic algorithms also become weaker with time, so implementations should be modular and ready for the set of mandatory algorithms to change.

For conformance, signer and verifier systems shall be able to process an electronic signature in accordance with the signature policy that the signature references by object identifier. Annex B explains that an implementation may hard-code one known policy, or may be dynamically programmable from a computer processable policy such as the ASN.1 form.
sections.eli5: If someone steals your pen, they can sign as you, so guard it well. Locks also get easier to pick as time passes, so you need to be able to swap in a stronger one.

items.label: clrCheck
items.desc: Check against current CRLs or authority revocation lists.

items.label: bothCheck
items.desc: Both CRL and OCSP checks must be carried out.

items.label: eitherCheck
items.desc: At least one of CRL or OCSP checks must be carried out.

items.label: other
items.desc: Other mechanism defined by a signature policy extension.
